The weather finally dropped below freezing the two nights prior, and the majority of lanternflies have died off, especially at this location. All the lanternflies we were using for the research project I've been working on died, at least (so field season is finally wrapping up). I saw 2 wild outliers at the research site on the day I took these photos, this was one of them. Still very lethargic from the cold, but it still had the energy to wave its front legs at me when I got close. 

(Also noteworthy: I checked another location later that day, where I knew there were numerous infested Ailanthus, to see if the lanternflies there had died off as well. I was surprised to find that more of those were still alive when I checked on them- considerably more than at the research site, at least. It wasn't that far away, but maybe that location was more sheltered or something, I'm not sure why more of them were still alive there.)

Details about this event from the Wild Ones Greater Baltimore eventbrite page:
After learning about native ferns during the June 15th Zoom presentation, join us for a field trip to view ferns growing in their natural habitats. During this hands-on experience guided by Judy Fulton you will learn about what different fern species look like and where they choose to grow.

This is a free event and limited to 15 participants.

Meeting details at Gunpowder Falls State Park will be provided to participants closer to the event date.

Event Guide Bio:
Judy Fulton, co-author of Plant Invaders of Mid-Atlantic Natural Areas, shares her knowledge via workshops, and serves as an expert in invasive plant litigation. Judy's lead role in creating the Mid-Atlantic Invaders Tool, an online guide to 900+ invasives, has positioned her as a sought-after advisor in eco-restoration.

Become an official Wild Ones member by visiting JoinWildOnesBaltimore.org

description:
There are claims circulating online that milkweed is toxic to spotted lanternflies though experts say there is no science to support this. However, I have observed that spotted lanternflies found on common milkweed (and presumptively have fed on it) exhibit altered responses to touch. Normally, SLFs on other plants will immediately jump and take a short flight before I can even grab the insect. However, the ones on milkweed seem very lethargic, don't move in response to being prodded or move feebly and they don't hop. Their responses seem staggered. 

Also see observations:

https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/183442869

There are claims circulating online that milkweed is toxic to spotted lanternflies though experts say there is no science to support this. However, I have observed that spotted lanternflies found on common milkweed (and presumptively have fed on it) in several different sites across several boroughs exhibit altered responses to touch. Normally, SLFs on other plants will immediately jump and take a short flight before I can even grab the insect. However, the ones on milkweed seem very lethargic, don't move in response to being prodded or move feebly and they don't hop. Their responses seem staggered.

I should not even be able to touch the insect like this since 1) it would have already hopped away and 2) would have actively struggled if I had caught onto it. 

Here it's not responding in a typical manner. After being touched, the specimen still did not hop or fly away which is quite bizarre.

Also see observations: 
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/183442869

description:
This is the second spotted lantern fly caught on my parents' farm. I have it in the same kind of jar next to the previous individual that I had caught and put into the freezer. So now they're roommates.

Unfortunately, while there was a third individual found in the driveway, I was not quick enough to catch it with a zip lock bag turned inside-out and used like a glove. Even if I did have a third jar, it was on some wild grape vines and maneuvering the jar to catch it would be very difficult if not impossible. They're too quick for me to kill on site. But for some reason, I have better luck catching them with a jar if they're on a flat(ish) surface.

Once the second one I've successfully caught succumbs to the cold, it will be transferred to the jar the previous one is in so I have a free catch-jar handy. I have not found anymore on the farm, at least not where I'd be comfortable looking, as there are quite a few carpenter bees and other large hymenopterans nearby I'd rather not anger.
